stories.headline: Ken Paxton Defeats John Cornyn in Texas Republican Senate Runoff
stories.summary:
Former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton defeated incumbent U.S. Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary runoff for the Texas U.S. Senate seat, with the race called by the Associated Press. Paxton, who survived a 2023 impeachment trial and has been a close Trump ally, credited the president directly in his victory speech, saying Trump stood by him "when everyone in Washington told him to abandon me." Cornyn, the former Senate Majority Whip, conceded and pledged to continue his Senate work through the end of his term.

The result sets up a general election matchup between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico, who appears headed toward winning his own runoff for the Democratic nomination. The race immediately raises questions for the Senate Leadership Fund, the Republican super PAC, which had not included Texas in its initial $342 million in ad reservations and will now face pressure to defend a state that was previously considered safe.

Paxton's victory is a significant test of Trump's continued grip on Republican primary voters and represents a rebuke of the Senate's establishment wing. Senator John Barrasso of Wyoming, the No. 2 Senate Republican who had backed Cornyn, quickly pivoted to endorse Paxton following the result. The outcome also has implications for Senate Republicans' slim majority heading into November.

The race drew coverage from 22 outlets across the political spectrum, making it one of the most-watched primary contests of the 2026 midterm cycle. In a separate Texas primary, Trump-backed congressional candidate Alex Mealer easily defeated state Representative Briscoe Cain in the Republican runoff for the state's Ninth Congressional District.

stories.headline: Congress Returns from Recess Facing Senate Vote on $70 Billion Immigration Bill, FISA Deadline, and Iran War Powers Resolution
stories.summary:
Congress reconvened Monday after a week-long Memorial Day recess with an unusually crowded legislative calendar. The Senate faces a delayed party-line vote on a $70 billion immigration bill after Republican objections to provisions including a Trump administration "anti-weaponization" fund and White House security upgrades. President Trump had set a June 1 deadline for the bill's passage, but leadership held off the vote amid intraparty dissent, with members including Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) and Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-CA) voicing opposition to the fund.

Also pressing is the expiration of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act reauthorization. The House previously passed a 45-day clean extension, but a longer-term deal remains under negotiation, widening a rift between the chambers. The House is also expected to bring up a war powers resolution that would force President Trump to end military hostilities with Iran — a measure that failed twice before but now appears more likely to pass after Rep. Jared Golden (D-ME), the lone Democratic holdout, signaled he would support it this time.

Additionally, bipartisan groups are preparing discharge petitions to force floor votes on $1.3 billion in Ukraine aid paired with new Russia sanctions, and on the Faster Labor Contracts Act, which would require employers to begin union contract bargaining within 10 days of certification. Discharge petitions bypass committee leadership, reflecting frustration among centrist members on both sides.

The week underscores the growing tension within the Republican coalition between Trump loyalists and traditional conservatives, a divide that former Vice President Mike Pence addressed in a Wall Street Journal op-ed criticizing Trump for abandoning conservative principles in favor of populism. Trump responded Sunday that the departure of more than 10,000 federal lawyers since late 2024 was "very good."

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Strikes Russian Fuel Infrastructure at Record Pace, Risking Moscow Fuel Crunch
stories.summary:
Ukraine carried out a record number of strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure in May, according to Bloomberg, raising the prospect of a significant fuel shortage inside Russia. The sustained campaign has targeted oil refineries, fuel depots, and logistics nodes that supply Russian military operations. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of conduct that may constitute a war crime in connection with the latest exchange of hostilities, marking the first time he has leveled that specific accusation in this phase of the conflict.

The strikes represent a meaningful escalation in Ukraine's strategic targeting doctrine, shifting from primarily battlefield interdiction toward degrading Russia's domestic energy supply chains. Analysts note that a sustained fuel crunch could constrain Russian armored and air operations, though Russia has shown resilience in rerouting supply chains in previous campaigns.

The development comes amid broader instability across multiple fronts. In Lebanon, Israel has continued its ground offensive and has seized the historic Beaufort Castle, with Prime Minister Netanyahu calling it a "decisive shift" in operations against Hezbollah. Separately, the U.S. and Iran are operating under a fragile 60-day ceasefire extension with Hormuz reopening terms still being finalized, even as both sides have reported fresh strikes near the strait.

The record Ukrainian strike tempo adds pressure to ongoing ceasefire and peace negotiation efforts in Europe and Washington, and could complicate Russian domestic politics as fuel costs and availability affect civilian life in addition to military readiness.

stories.headline: Update: PSG Victory Parade Proceeds Peacefully as France Tallies Riot Damage — 780 Arrested, 219 Injured
stories.summary:
French authorities reported 780 arrests and 219 injuries — including 57 police officers — following riots that erupted overnight after Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League victory over Arsenal. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said eight people were in serious condition. A 24-year-old was found dead near the Paris ring road, which rioters attempted to block; the exact circumstances of his death remain under investigation. A teenager was also in critical condition following a separate brawl.

Despite the overnight violence, Monday's official victory parade proceeded without major incident. PSG players and staff toured the Champ-de-Mars near the Eiffel Tower before attending a reception at the Élysée Palace hosted by President Emmanuel Macron. Some 6,000 police were deployed for the celebration. Nuñez acknowledged the vast majority of fans celebrated peacefully, but blamed organized troublemakers — not PSG supporters — for the violence.

The scale of the unrest mirrors disturbances following PSG's Champions League title last year, raising questions about France's ability to manage large-scale sporting celebrations. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen criticized the government on social media, writing: "Only in France does a football club's victory spark riots." The interior minister defended security forces, saying France has strong capacity for public order but will not tolerate excess.

Officials noted that offenses ranged from attacks on police to weapons possession and theft. Paris police made 480 of the total arrests, with 277 taken into custody including 82 minors. The incidents are expected to intensify political debate in France about public security and the policing of large sporting events ahead of the FIFA World Cup, which opens June 11.
